references.text: Wisdom cries out in the streets and squares, inviting all to come – a parallel to the Lord's command to go out into the roads and invite people to enter ([ref:Prov 1:20-23|Proverbs 1:20-23]).
God's universal invitation to all who are thirsty to come and eat and drink – a parallel to the parable's invitation to the feast, now extended to all ([ref:Isa 55:1-2|Isaiah 55:1-2]).
The preceding part of the parable where the Lord first sends his servants out into the city streets and alleys to bring in the poor, crippled, blind, and lame ([ref:Lk 14:21|Luke 14:21]).

Paul and Barnabas turn to the Gentiles after the Jews reject the gospel – a fulfillment of the parable's principle to go out to others when the first invited refuse to come ([ref:Acts 13:46-47|Acts 13:46-47]).
Paul turns from the Jews to the Gentiles in Corinth, reflecting the parable's movement from those originally invited to those outside ([ref:Acts 18:6|Acts 18:6]).
Paul declares that God's salvation has been sent to the Gentiles – a thematic parallel to the servant being sent out into the roads to fill the house ([ref:Acts 28:28|Acts 28:28]).

In Matthew's parallel parable of the wedding feast, servants are sent out to the crossroads to invite everyone they find, both bad and good, so that the wedding hall is filled ([ref:Matt 22:9-10|Matthew 22:9-10]).

Paul explains that Israel's fall led to salvation for the Gentiles – this reflects the parable's structure where the first invited reject the invitation and others are brought in instead ([ref:Rom 11:11-12|Romans 11:11-12]).

The promise to Abraham that all families of the earth will be blessed through him – the parable points to the universal scope of God's invitation, which includes all peoples ([ref:Gen 12:3|Genesis 12:3]).
Paul urges and pleads on Christ's behalf that people should be reconciled to God – a parallel to the urgent appeal "compel them to come in" ([ref:2 Cor 5:20|2 Corinthians 5:20]).
